description:
We are Team ORI SPACE 🚀 at NASA Space Apps!
Inspired by the word 'Origin' and the mighty 'Orion' constellation, we are a dynamic team of innovators ready to be the starting point for groundbreaking ideas. Powered by NASA’s open data and a passion for technology, we aim to transform complex challenges into real-world solutions for Earth and beyond. The journey begins here, and our ambition knows no limits! ✨🌍
summary:
Ori Space is an educational website that brings the tales of NASA’s space exploration equipment to life for school children. The website has 13 pieces of equipment grouped into illustrated story pages ranging from lunar modules to rovers. Landers and spacecraft that have gone beyond Mars. Children can choose where they want to visit and which piece of equipment they would like to explore. They will learn why it was created, how it worked, what scientists discovered, and what happened after its mission.

This project tackles the ‘Abandoned but not Forgotten’ challenge by linking the abandoned equipment to the scientific discoveries it has made possible. We use resources from NASA to help explain the complex history of each mission in easy-to-understand language. Using visuals helps engage children with the information. There is also a Games section which includes activities related to each mission to allow the children to engage with the stories again and put their knowledge to the test.

Ori Space shows the lasting impact of exploring space. Even when the equipment stops working, the discoveries made will still impact how we understand the universe. We want to create an interest in science and engineering and help children feel like they can be future explorers.
details:
Ori Space is a website aimed at helping school students learn more about the background of equipment used in space exploration by NASA. This website explains why space missions took place, how the equipment works, what has been learnt by the scientists, and what happened once the mission ended.

 

This website helps solve the problem ‘Abandoned but not Forgotten’ by showcasing the importance of the equipment left on the Moon, Mars, or other areas of space. Although the mission may have finished, this equipment has helped us learn so much about our solar system and universe.

 

How the Website Works:

 

The website starts with the welcome page, which includes the name and logo of the Ori Space team. From here, you can choose to look at either the Moon or Mars section. You can click through to view cards with images and names of the equipment. When you click on a card, you will be taken to a page with an illustrated story. Once you have finished reading this story, you can click the buttons to navigate back to the equipment and look at a different mission.

 

The website has 13 different pieces of equipment. The Moon section includes the Apollo Lunar Module, Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP Scientific Packages, and Surveyor Landers. The Mars and beyond section includes Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Viking 1 & 2, Phoenix and InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer 10 and 11, and Kepler. This allows students to learn about other missions outside of Mars such as asteroids, outer planets, and planets orbiting far-away stars.

 

Each piece of equipment has a story with four main sections. The first section asks why the equipment was made, the second asks how it works, the third asks what the scientists have learnt from it, and finally what happened after the mission. The paragraphs and images help tell the story of key points throughout the mission whilst also linking to the technical facts.

 

Learning Through Games:

 

We have created a specific games section which allows users to complete activities relating to each mission. This helps students to consolidate their knowledge.

 

For example, the Phoenix and InSight activity has eight multiple-choice questions. Each question has a scoring system and rocket thrust. If the answer is correct, the rocket will have more thrust. This helps students to link their learning to a fun and simple game.

 

Development Tools:

 

HTML and CSS were used to create the main website. Visual Studio Code was used to write, organize, and edit the code. HTML helped format the website with headings, paragraphs, images and links. CSS helped format the website with colors, fonts and simple animations.

 

Google Sites was used to host the linked activities and stories. Resources from NASA were used to help with the missions. We used an AI to help us brainstorm, code, debug, and edit the descriptions. We chose the resources ourselves.

 

The website can be used on any browser and does not require any specific hardware. The website has a dark space-themed background, contrasting text, and orange buttons. The images are to scale and responsive to help users navigate through different screen sizes. There are gentle animations to introduce the content and settings, and reduced motion can be used to prevent unwanted movement.

 

Creative Elements:

 

The website has been designed creatively to help students see the equipment as a journey. For example, the rover has been turned into an explorer looking at the rocks, whilst the lander has been turned into a science station. The telescope helps the student learn how the engineering decisions helped the scientists make new discoveries. The stories help students understand why the equipment was designed the way it was.

 

We thought about the audience (school-age), using simple English, scientific accuracy, placement of images, navigation, and readability. We made sure long stories had short paragraphs. Images were placed with the relevant event. We thought about how easy it would be for students to navigate to different places, read the stories, and complete activities.

 

Impact:

 

The goal of Ori Space is to help make space science more accessible and spark an interest in engineering, astronomy, and exploration. The website can be used for self-learning or can be used as a starting point for discussion in class about how scientists explore unknown environments.

 

It also helps students understand that the equipment can still be valuable even though the mission has finished. The equipment does not have to be working to still be important; the measurements, discoveries, and engineering can help with future exploration. Ori Space shows that although the mission has ended, the discoveries can still inspire future explorers.
